tagline: A buried ambush hunter with spring-loaded jaws
summary: A giant bristle worm that hides almost its whole body in a mucus-lined burrow, leaving only five striped antennae above the sand. When a fish touches them, its jaws snap shut and drag the prey underground. Recorded specimens approach 3 m long, which makes it a contender for the longest polychaete.

stats.size: Longest recorded specimen about 3 m (299 cm)
stats.depth: Shallow, warm coastal seabeds: intertidal to subtidal sand, rubble and rock
stats.range: Warm waters of the Indo-Pacific and Atlantic (identity of many records uncertain)

facts.title: Antennae as bait
facts.text: By day it lies buried with five striped antennae poking out. These sense passing prey and may also work as a lure. Its jaws wait under tension like a sprung trap.

facts.title: Changes tactics at night
facts.text: After dark, it switches from waiting to actively hunting, pushing out of its burrow to snatch passing prey.

facts.title: Fish fight back
facts.text: In Indonesia's Lembeh Strait, groups of young monocle bream were seen 'mobbing' bobbit worms, squirting jets of water at the burrow until the worm sometimes retreated.

facts.title: A 20-million-year-old lair
facts.text: L-shaped fossil burrows up to 2 m long, found in Miocene rocks in Taiwan, closely resemble bobbit worm lairs. They suggest ambush-hunting worms like this were already present about 20 million years ago.

facts.title: Probably several species
facts.text: Many different giant worms have been lumped under this name. Taxonomists warn that some 'bobbit worms' worldwide may be other, even undescribed, species.

references.title: Novel mobbing strategies of a fish population against a sessile annelid predator — Lachat & Haag-Wackernagel 2016

image.alt: The head of a large worm rising from dark gravelly sand. Its tan, iridescent body segments shimmer blue and green, curved grey jaws spread open, and five striped antennae stick straight up.
image.caption: A bobbit worm with its jaws open, Anilao, Philippines.
image.creator: Rickard Zerpe

notes: WoRMS gives Eunice aphroditois (Pallas, 1788) as the accepted name. Its type locality is Sri Lanka and no type specimen exists. Per the ZooKeys 2022 paper, Indo-Pacific 'bobbit worms' are almost always identified as E. aphroditois, but this name has absorbed several giant species. The hero photo (Philippines) follows that convention; its true species identity cannot be confirmed from a photo. Commons iNaturalist images of slim reddish worms on rock, and a fish-like image ('Eunice aphroditois 33864655'), were rejected. The 299 cm figure is the record specimen cited in Lachat & Haag-Wackernagel 2016. We did not use the popular story that the name refers to females severing males' genitals: no source supports it. Depth is not given in the sources consulted; depthRange 0–40 m is an indicative value for shallow coastal habitat.
